claims.statement: Jurançon is a Pyrenean-foothill white-wine AOP centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng, with established dry and sweet traditions.

claims.label: Jurançon landscape
claims.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

claims.label: Dry + sweet
claims.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

claims.label: Three legal paths
claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

claims.label: Principal + accessory grapes
claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

claims.label: Harvest changes the path
claims.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

claims.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
claims.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

claims.label: Wine-growing communes
claims.statement: INAO describes the Jurançon production area across 25 communes between Pau and the Pyrenees.

claims.label: Member vineyards
claims.statement: The Vignerons du Jurançon association reports 620 hectares of member vineyards; this is not represented as the total AOP vineyard area.
Jurançon is a French AOP documented by INAO.

INAO describes Jurançon as hillside viticulture at the Pyrenean foothills under an oceanic climate with a frequent warm, dry southerly autumn wind; sweet wines were recognized in 1936 and dry Jurançon in 1975, with hand harvesting linked to high-trained vines and steep terrain.
INAO describes Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng as the principal local grape varieties of Jurançon.

location.description: INAO describes Jurançon as hillside and terrace viticulture in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence. CARTA separately links the INAO 2026-08-24 cartographic representation of the regulatory geographical area.

claims.statement: Plantgrape describes Courbu as an autochthonous Pyrenean cultivar that is wind-sensitive, generally suited to long pruning, susceptible to grey rot, and capable of sugar-rich musts with moderate acidity and fine wines.
Plantgrape states that Courbu is officially designated Hondarrabi Zuri in Spain, while Gros Courbu is an official propagation-material alternative in France.

Plantgrape identifies Gros Manseng as originating in Pyrenean vineyards; it is vigorous and fertile, sensitive to powdery mildew, and relatively resistant to grey rot, with fruit able to remain on the vine for sweet-wine production.

The Profetas producer identifies Listrão as the Porto Santo/Madeira name for the grape also known as Listán Blanco and Palomino Fino; CARTA reuses the existing Palomino Fino grape identity rather than creating a duplicate Listrão entity.
Plantgrape treats Petit Courbu as a distinct Pyrenean cultivar and lists no officially recognized propagation synonym in France or other EU countries on its record.

Plantgrape describes Petit Courbu as an autochthonous Pyrenean cultivar of low productivity that generally requires long pruning, has small clusters and very small berries, and is susceptible to grey rot; its wines can be fine and aromatic.

The current Bizkaiko Txakolina specification presents Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia together with Petit Courbu as a recommended/main white variety, creating a jurisdiction-specific legal-name equivalence that should not automatically be generalized into universal synonymy.

claims.statement: Plantgrape reports published genetic analyses indicating Petit Manseng is closely related to Savagnin; this is a closeness claim, not a resolved parent-offspring statement in the evidence captured here.

Plantgrape places Petit Manseng's origin in Pyrénées-Atlantiques and describes very small berries, very high acid retention despite strong sugar concentration, vigor requiring trellising/long pruning, and very strong grey-rot resistance.

Current Virginia Wine Board research includes a dedicated 'In Pursuit of Dry Petit Manseng' project, supporting the narrower claim that dry Petit Manseng is an active technical and stylistic research subject in Virginia.

Virginia Tech trials found Petit Manseng's loose clusters and very small berries associated with very low fruit-rot incidence in test years, while older Virginia trials documented high Brix alongside substantial retained acidity.

A 2025 Virginia Tech study reported Petit Manseng total soluble solids increasing from 8.0 to 23.6 Brix while titratable acidity declined from 25 to 10.8 g/L, with acid depletion plateauing about two weeks after sugar accumulation plateaued in the studied fruit.

claims.statement: Plantgrape lists Blauer Spätburgunder as the officially recognized German alternative name for Pinot noir in European propagation-material contexts.

The German Wine Institute treats Spätburgunder and Pinot Noir as names for the same grape variety; CARTA therefore keeps the bottle wording Pinot Noir while governing Spätburgunder on the existing Pinot Noir grape identity.
Plantgrape reports Raffiat de Moncade as probably resulting from a cross between Gouais blanc and Bouchalès.

Savagnin is a wine grape, not a cellar method. CARTA's primary sources separately document it in topped, non-oxidative wine, Jura's sous-voile and vin-jaune context, and sparkling-wine rules, so the grape name alone does not tell you how the wine was raised.

claims.label: Same Energy · film yeast, different worlds
claims.statement: CARTA's sources document Savagnin in Jura's sous-voile and vin-jaune context and Palomino Fino in The Flor of Evangelho's flor-aging context. Their shared film-yeast axis supports a Same Energy bridge while their grapes, legal frameworks and wine cultures remain distinct.

claims.label: A local name
claims.statement: Plantgrape records Naturé as an officially recognized French synonym for Savagnin blanc.

claims.statement: Beaujolais is a 12-AOC region built around two broad appellations and ten northern crus, with Gamay at its center but meaningful differences in geology, exposure and origin.

claims.label: Why Beaujolais matters
claims.statement: Beaujolais shows how one dominant grape can still yield a region of distinct places: broad Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages context surrounds ten individually named crus.

claims.label: How to read the hierarchy
claims.statement: The ten crus occupy the northern half of the region; Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages provide the broader appellation frame and can include red, white and rosé wines.

claims.label: A varied physical place
claims.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

Jura is a compact eastern French wine region whose six wine AOPs form three overlapping families: geographic still-wine origins, traditional-method Crémant du Jura, and fortified Macvin du Jura.

claims.label: Why Jura matters
claims.statement: Jura makes legal hierarchy, grape identity and winemaking method unusually easy to compare in one small place: Chardonnay and Savagnin whites, three red grapes, vin jaune, sparkling wine and mistelle all coexist without meaning the same thing.

claims.label: Physical place
claims.statement: The Jura vineyard forms a narrow north–south band along the western foothills of the Jura mountains, with varied slopes and exposures rather than one uniform site.

claims.label: How to read the hierarchy
claims.statement: Arbois, Côtes du Jura, L’Etoile and Château-Chalon are geographic AOPs; Crémant du Jura and Macvin du Jura overlap that geography but govern different wine categories and methods.

claims.label: The wine picture
claims.statement: Côtes du Jura permits white, red, rosé and vin jaune; Crémant du Jura is traditional-method sparkling wine; Macvin du Jura is a white, red or rosé liqueur wine. These are distinct legal styles, not interchangeable labels.

claims.statement: The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

claims.label: Why Loire matters
claims.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

claims.label: How to read the place
claims.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

claims.label: InterLoire scope
claims.statement: InterLoire reports 42,000 hectares across its own 34-AOP and one-IGP operating scope; this is not a total for every Loire vineyard.

claims.statement: Spanish Wine Lover reports Egia's Egia Enea vineyard as two south-facing hectares around 225 metres, divided into three plots planted in 2001; CARTA treats this as a documented historical vineyard description rather than a permanent total-estate-size claim.

Across current producer reporting, Egia's cellar work is described as spontaneous fermentation with extended lees contact and use of neutral or older vessels including barrel and, for some wines, amphora; sulfur practice is wine- and vintage-specific and should not be generalized as universally zero-sulfur.
Alfredo Egia's producer work is associated with vineyards in Balmaseda within Bizkaiko Txakolina.

Current specialist and trade reporting documents Egia Enea, Lexardi, Rebel Rebel, Izaki and the Hegan Egin collaboration as useful anchors for understanding Alfredo Egia's range and collaborative work.

Current importer descriptions document whole-cluster direct pressing, spontaneous barrel/amphora fermentation, extended lees aging, some intentionally untopped élevage, and very low or no added sulfur depending on vintage, making Rebel Rebel structurally atypical relative to the light, brisk txakoli stereotype without proving it is historically unprecedented.
Alfredo Egia describes Imanol Garay's experience as guiding the collaborative path; trade sources explicitly characterize Garay as Egia's friend and mentor.

Hegan Egin is a collaboration among Alfredo Egia, Imanol Garay, and Gile Iturriondobeitia, with Garay contributing low-intervention know-how, Gile working as winemaker, and Egia as viticulturist in Egia's 2022 account.
On 2026-08-18, Buvons Wine showed 2020 Alfredo Egia Rebel Rebel at $72 with two bottles explicitly shown in stock.
On 2026-08-18, Leon & Son displayed a price of $69.99 for 2021 Alfredo Egia Rebel Rebel.
On 2026-08-18, Leon & Son marked its 2021 Alfredo Egia Rebel Rebel listing Sold Out.

location.description: Producer work is associated with vineyards in and around Balmaseda, Bizkaia. This is municipality/locality-level placement, not a vineyard point.

claims.label: Jurançon base
claims.statement: Camin Larredya publishes its estate address at Chapelle de Rousse, 1901 Chemin Larredya, in the commune of Jurançon; CARTA maps that production base, not its vineyard parcels or purchased-fruit sources.

claims.label: Terraces + local grapes
claims.statement: Camin Larredya describes a 9.5-hectare certified-organic estate, including 4 hectares of terraces, planted mainly to Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng with Petit Courbu and Camaralet completing the estate mix.
Camin Larredya's own materials document work with Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Petit Courbu and Camaralet, making the estate a useful anchor for understanding Jurançon's local white-grape mix.

location.description: Camin Larredya’s published estate address is shown at Chapelle de Rousse in Jurançon. This is a production-base point, not a parcel, vineyard or fruit-source map.

claims.label: Monein · a visible style range
claims.statement: Clos Uroulat publishes its base in Monein’s Quartier Trouilh; the current departmental tourism record describes a six-wine visitor range spanning three dry wines, one tender wine and two sweet wines.

location.description: Clos Uroulat’s published domaine base is shown in Monein’s Quartier Trouilh. This is a production-base point, not a parcel or vineyard map.

claims.label: Monein · dry + sweet
claims.statement: Domaine Cauhapé describes a Monein estate on southeast-facing Jurançon slopes, with vineyards rising to about 400 metres and a range that deliberately includes both dry and sweet wines.

location.description: Domaine Cauhapé is shown approximately at its published Monein estate locality. This orientation point is not a parcel or vineyard map.

Domaine de la Tournelle publishes its domaine base at 5 Petite Place in Arbois.

Domaine de la Tournelle Fleur de Savagnin is a distinct persistent wine from Domaine Labet's same-named wine; the producer describes it as 100% Savagnin from grey marl and deliberately ouillé/non-oxidative.

claims.statement: Domaine de Saint Pierre is the Mathenay, Jura estate associated with Fabrice Dodane. Dodane joined as manager in 1989 and later acquired/took control of the estate; specialist sources differ between 2011 and 2012 for the transfer, so CARTA does not force an exact takeover year.
Ecocert currently lists Fabrice Dodane / Domaine de Saint-Pierre in Mathenay under EU organic agriculture certification.

Château Renard is a recurring white Arbois bottling of Domaine de Saint Pierre / Fabrice Dodane. Available vintage records show that its detailed composition should be temporalized rather than treated as permanently 100% Chardonnay.
Beaune Imports identifies the 2018 Château Renard as Arbois Chardonnay from Domaine de Saint Pierre / Fabrice Dodane.

location.description: Domaine de Saint Pierre is shown approximately at the Mathenay commune centre because current evidence supports a municipality base, not a verified street address. This is not a vineyard map.

location.description: Domaine de Souch’s association-published estate address is shown in Laroin. This is a production-base point, not a parcel or vineyard map.

claims.statement: Domaine Labet is a family wine estate based in Rotalier in the southern Jura / Sud-Revermont; the Jura interprofessional profile documents 13.5 hectares across 45 parcels in four communes.
The Jura interprofessional profile identifies Alain, Julien, Charline and Romain Labet among the family vignerons of Domaine Labet.
The commune of Rotalier lists Domaine Labet at 14 Montée des Tilleuls, consistent with the Jura interprofessional profile's identification of the estate as based in Rotalier.

For the 2022 La Bardette Chardonnay, specialist retail/importer notes describe a 0.5-hectare west-facing La Bardette parcel planted in 1947 and more than 30 months of aging in used 228-litre barrels; the estate's broader La Bardette holdings include plantings of other ages, so this detail is scoped to the 2022 single-parcel bottling.
Domaine Labet's Fleur de Savagnin is documented as a Savagnin blend assembled from multiple Lias-marl parcels rather than a single vineyard wine; the listed plantings span multiple years and sites.

The Jura interprofessional profile describes La Cuvée du Hasard as Chardonnay from vines older than 60 years, blended from different Lias-marl terroirs and aged sous voile in old 228-litre pièces for 36 to 48 months.

claims.statement: Beattie & Roberts reports roughly one hectare of Garay's own vines in Saint-Étienne-de-Baïgorry just outside Irouléguy, another roughly one hectare near Orthez, and additional purchased fruit from Madiran and Spanish sites; owned/farmed vines and purchased fruit must remain distinct in CARTA.
Current importer documentation describes Imanol Garay as farming biodynamically and vinifying with native fermentations and very low-intervention cellar practice across his French and Spanish work.
Current importer documentation describes Garay using a mixed cellar of barrels, tanks and amphorae rather than one fixed vessel regime.
The 2023 Ixilune description differs materially from earlier documented vintages, reinforcing that Ixilune's grape composition and cellar treatment are vintage-specific rather than a timeless recipe.

Imanol Garay's Ixilune has been documented in different vintages as a blend centered on Raffiat de Moncade with Petit Manseng and Petit Courbu, and sometimes Gros Manseng; blend proportions and maceration vary by vintage.
Beattie & Roberts documents Clandestinus 2022 as one of Imanol Garay's representative wines, providing a distinct reference point from his white cuvées.
Beattie & Roberts documents La Altannativa 2021 as a Garay wine made from purchased Madiran Tannat, making it a useful anchor for distinguishing estate vines from purchased-fruit work.

Hegan Egin is a collaboration among Alfredo Egia, Imanol Garay, and Gile Iturriondobeitia, with Garay contributing low-intervention know-how, Gile working as winemaker, and Egia as viticulturist in Egia's 2022 account.
Multiple trade sources report that Imanol Garay worked with Richard Leroy before establishing his own project.

claims.label: A story of transmission
claims.statement: Louis/Dressner presents the Pupillin estate as a story of transmission: Pierre Overnoy took over family vines in 1968; Emmanuel Houillon trained and worked there through the 1990s and says he took over the estate in 2001.

claims.label: IYKYK · read the wax
claims.statement: Louis/Dressner describes a house label code in which most regular Overnoy cuvées share the same front label: wax color distinguishes Chardonnay, Savagnin and Ploussard, 50 cl identifies topped Savagnin in the profile, and bottling dates added since 2018 help distinguish separate releases of one vintage.

claims.label: Access is context, not a score
claims.statement: Louis/Dressner states that its United States allocation of Overnoy is fewer than 400 bottles a year for the whole country. CARTA treats that as dated importer-market context: scarcity explains access pressure but does not prove quality or educational value.

The French public business register lists GAEC Emmanuel Houillon Overnoy as an active grape-growing business based in Pupillin; Louis/Dressner identifies the wine estate as Emmanuel Houillon / Maison Pierre Overnoy.
Louis/Dressner's current estate profile lists Chardonnay, Savagnin, Ploussard and Trousseau among the grapes grown by Emmanuel Houillon / Maison Pierre Overnoy.

claims.label: The earlier chapter
claims.statement: Louis/Dressner reports that Pierre Overnoy took over the family's vineyard portion in Pupillin in 1968, later trained and worked with Emmanuel Houillon, and retired in 2001 while remaining present around the family and estate.

claims.label: Part of the lineage
claims.statement: Louis/Dressner's profile and Emmanuel Houillon interview document Houillon beginning his apprenticeship with Pierre Overnoy in 1990, returning full-time in 1997, and taking over the estate in 2001 after years of working and learning alongside Overnoy.

location.description: Maison Pierre Overnoy / Emmanuel Houillon is shown at its active public business-register address in Pupillin. This is a production-base point, not a vineyard map.

claims.statement: Soleras del Pacífico is Jake Neustadt's project, begun from the opportunity in 2017 to work with old Palomino vines at Evangelho Vineyard while he was working as a Bedrock Wine Co. viticulturist.

Evangelho Vineyard in Contra Costa County was planted in the 1890s on deep sandy soils; Soleras del Pacífico documents just over 100 Palomino vines there, while Bedrock identifies itself as the vineyard owner and farmer.

The Flor of Evangelho is documented as a single-vineyard Palomino Fino wine in a fino-style solera established in 2017: native barrel fermentation is followed by light spring fortification to favor flor, fractional blending through a four-level solera, maturation under flor and unfiltered bottling.
